props.title: Cleopatra
props.initialSlug: Seductive queen gambles Egypt's fate for power & love

sections.content: Cecil B. DeMille's Cleopatra revolutionized historical epics with its daring Pre-Code sensuality and lavish Art Deco aesthetics. Claudette Colbert's fierce, sultry portrayal broke from the stuffy Victorian interpretations, showing Cleopatra as a cunning political strategist rather than just a seductress. The film's massive sets and provocative costume design by Travis Banton, particularly the infamous milk bath scene, influenced Hollywood's vision of ancient Egypt for decades. This preceded the even more extravagant The Ten Commandments (1956) and Elizabeth Taylor's Cleopatra. Ben-Hur|1959|Charlton Heston's epic revenge tale set in Roman times, featuring the legendary chariot race sequence|Prime The Egyptian|1954|Lavish historical drama about an ancient physician rising to power in the Pharaoh's court|Criterion Spartacus|1960|Stanley Kubrick's Roman epic starring Kirk Douglas as the legendary slave who led a rebellion|Netflix

The 1930s saw a fascinating surge in ancient world epics, with The Sign of the Cross (1932) and Cleopatra pushing boundaries of sexuality and violence before the Production Code crackdown. DeMille's innovative use of miniatures and practical effects, especially in the naval battle sequences, established techniques that would influence historical epics for generations. The film's blend of historical drama with contemporary Art Deco styling created a unique visual language that later appeared in films like Land of the Pharaohs (1955).

Claudette Colbert's performance marked a crucial shift in how ancient female rulers were portrayed on screen. Unlike the melodramatic takes of earlier silents like Cleopatra, Colbert brought a modern, sophisticated edge that influenced later performances, from Vivien Leigh in Caesar and Cleopatra (1945) to Elizabeth Taylor's iconic portrayal. The film's success also paved the way for other female-led historical epics like The Private Life of Henry VIII (1933). Quo Vadis|1951|Spectacular Roman epic about Emperor Nero's persecution of Christians, starring Peter Ustinov|TCM The Fall of the Roman Empire|1964|Sophisticated historical drama about Rome's decline, featuring stunning set pieces|Prime SUBHEAD: The Art Deco Influence on Historical Epics

DeMille's bold choice to incorporate Art Deco elements into ancient Egyptian settings created a distinctive visual style that influenced set design for decades. The geometric patterns and modernist touches in Cleopatra's palace scenes inspired later films like The Ten Commandments (1956) and even echoed in modern interpretations like Exodus: Gods and Kings (2014). This artistic approach demonstrated how historical films could be both period-accurate and contemporarily relevant.
